extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers, social critics, educators, and reformers (early 20th-century British context)
extracted.subtask_description: A polemical essay assessing the moral and practical failings of English public schools, modern elementary/ female education, philanthropy, collectivist ideologies, and political reform; argues for principle-based progress, respect for popular traditions, and preservation of individual/family life. Extracts normative claims and standards embedded in Chesterton's prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth / Veracity as a primary virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The English public-school man and Parliament care for everything except veracity; truth is often absent from the character produced by public schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: cultivating politeness, courage, neatness, and social graces while neglecting honesty; producing 'gentlemen' who are untruthful in private or public life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish pleasure/convenience from moral virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not mistake agreeable or convenient practices (like washing or sport) for genuine moral virtues; pleasures of the gentleman have been reframed as virtues without principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the 'superstition of soap' — cleanliness portrayed as moral purity. Anti-patterns: equating physical cleanliness or athleticism with moral goodness; praising activities because they are pleasant rather than principled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating class comforts with universal moral standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Upper-class habits (e.g., bathing, sport, organized charity) are often presented as universally applicable virtues though they arise from luxury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: evaluate whether an ideal stems from class convenience; beware applying aristocratic rituals (linen, cast-off clothes ritual) to the poor without adapting to their realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct, personal charity over paternalistic organized philanthropy
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of philanthropists who disdain direct gifts to beggars while boasting of brooding over institutional solutions; giving a penny directly can be as valuable as elaborate institutional plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: refusing to deal directly with beggars on the ground that charity is 'easy' and instead creating distant institutions; remedy: personal engagement — 'talking to the ten beggars who come to his door.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress must be principle-based, not precedent-driven
rubrics_metrics.description: Real progress should stem from principles and first principles; modern progress too often follows precedent and admitted practice rather than theoretical justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: incremental 'progress by precedent' where reforms simply reproduce past admitted practices (e.g., lowering closing hours, raising school-leaving age repeatedly). Anti-pattern: confusing momentum of practice with moral rightness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of reform that merely conserves previous reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Conservatives often defend situations rather than ideals; revolutionaries create reforms while conservatives merely conserve the reform and never reform the reform when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: evaluators should ask whether a reform preserves an ideal or merely fossilizes a contingent change into dogma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational ideals must suit the lives of the poor
rubrics_metrics.description: Elementary (democratic) education should not import the ethical prejudices and impractical ideals of elite public schools; many 'healthy' ideals are inappropriate for an impoverished democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: preaching cleanliness where poverty makes it impractical; glorifying organized sport to people who already have manual labor exercise; disdain or suppression of spontaneous, patchwork generosity characteristic of the poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and incorporate parental and popular traditions in schooling
rubrics_metrics.description: Schools often ignore the opinions and traditions of parents (especially poor parents); yet those traditions (coarse speech about vice, open mourning rituals, popular humor) embody human values and psychological truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: educational practice should consult and respect parents' customs; anti-pattern: treating the master as 'in loco parentis' for the rich while being 'contra parentem' for the poor, thereby 'handing down the customs of the minority' and 'rooting out the customs of the majority.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge the value of popular mourning and communal expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Working-class open display and gossip at bereavements (funeral feasts, loud lament) are psychologically sound ways to lessen sorrow and deserve recognition rather than suppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the poor's funeral customs as 'priests of the universal civilization'; anti-pattern: treating bereavement as a private disgrace not to be publicly discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should not aim to erase the character and pride of the poor
rubrics_metrics.description: Schoolmasters should not attempt to eradicate the 'rugged legends' and point-of-honor of working people; education should not promote disdain for local honor codes or practical dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: preaching soap and Socialism against beer and liberty; promoting 'hazy advice' to the poor who have no money; failing to teach sympathy for father's irony or mother's pietas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female education requires its own ideal, not mere imitation of male schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: The new female education is just a copy of what is done to boys (football, colors, heavy homework) and lacks an intellectual design appropriate to sex and social function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: consider whether bodily and social practices good for men are appropriate for women; retain valuable amateur ideals of the older 'elegant female' rather than forcing male formats (heavy homework, brutal games).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of the 'universal amateur' (one great amateur) in culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Society needs at least one great amateur — a non-specialist who renounces narrow conquest to 'conquer all the conquerors' and so remain queen/king of life; amateurish breadth preserves vital human qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: preference for the old 'elegant female' with shaky Italian and water-colors as an intelligible idea over the new woman with no coherent ideal. Anti-pattern: universal specialization with everyone becoming an artist/professional and losing general humanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should cultivate 'fiery simplicity' — levity and spontaneous delight
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim of education is to pour 'fiery simplicity' upon life: maintaining childlike joy, amateurish audacity, and the ability to sing, paint, or garden with equal gusto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: solemnity and pretentious long words replacing spontaneous feeling; excluding humor about appearance and death from polite culture removes half the healthy literature of the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uphold individual human worth against collectivist 'hive' ideologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the glorification of insect-like collective morality (the 'Soul of the Hive') that prizes communal ends over the intrinsic worth of one good and happy man; oppose political or social movements that model human society on bees/ants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: critique of Maeterlinck's bee-worship and of ideologies that praise nations as hive-like; warning that such thought dissolves the idea of the human family and risks making the hive larger than the house.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not strengthen the state at the expense of the family and personal liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Social reforms often 'mend' the state (sharpen machinery, centralize power) while leaving the family in ruins; reformers should avoid increasing despotic public power over private life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: a Socialist treats a walking-stick like an umbrella because both go into the umbrella-stand — superficially similar things are fundamentally different. Beware reforms that increase coercive government (e.g., schemes that place many people 'in the despotic power of Mr. Bumble').

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish clearly between private and public spheres in reform
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a vital difference between what should be mended (private, familial institutions) and what should be ended (despotic institutions); reformers must have an instinctive sense of what is private and what is public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: mending implies strengthening something one values (like the family), while ending is appropriate for things one dislikes (like oligarchy). Anti-pattern: confusing or conflating spheres and thereby eroding personal liberty.
